title: Python Architecture and Request Lifecycle
text: Python Architecture and Request Lifecycle Read the new Rust-owned pipeline architecture . The sections below also describe the retained legacy integration. Django, Flask, and FastAPI expose separate adapters over the shared Python core. The adapter owns framework execution; the core supplies route policies, state abstractions, detection helpers, and training primitives. On this page Native CSV request engine Legacy adapter architecture Module boundaries Initialization and policy planning How each adapter executes Following one request Live routes, manifests, and decorators Storage and reputation Training and scoring The Rust acceleration boundary Worked example: an API request and a scanner Trace the implementation How AIWAF works: system architecture Rust-owned CSV request lifecycle Release candidate: this page documents Python 1.1.8 and Rust/Python 0.2.7 in the current source checkout. Source versions do not establish registry availability. Python 1.1.8 requires aiwaf-rust>=0.2.7 ; framework dependencies remain extras. Install the explicit native adapter instead of the existing AIWAF middleware chain. Installing the required Rust dependency does not automatically switch existing applications to this pipeline. Legacy adapters remain available for custom stores and hooks; their configuration and fallback behavior are separate. Rust owns the native CSV pipeline configuration, enforcement order, SQL and keyword inspection, geo/blocklist decisions, rate buckets, form timing, UUID scores, anomaly history/inference, keyword learning, and CSV logging. Python supplies framework routes, authentication facts, GeoIP lookup, bounded request buffering, and response construction. Training and management still have Python interfaces. Initialize once Validate the native API, immutable profile and CSV schemas; optionally load a trained model snapshot. Extract framework facts Python resolves routes, methods, decorators, authentication and country; buffers a bounded body and normalizes headers. Begin in Rust One engine call applies enabled request stages and returns an opaque context plus an allow or denial decision. Run the application Python dispatches allowed requests or constructs the rejection response. Finish in Rust One response call updates UUID/anomaly state, learns eligible 404 keywords and appends the CSV log. Enforcement order geo_block → ip_keyword_block → rate_limit → ai_anomaly → honeypot → uuid_tamper → header_validation → logging . Request checks run before the handler; response-dependent UUID/anomaly observation and logging run during finalization. Model scoring sees the response outcome and can update state for later requests; it cannot retract a response already sent. Boundaries and guarantees The engine has no Python policy callbacks or Python execution fallback. Missing native API, invalid schemas, unknown profile keys and unsupported settings fail at startup. Bounded structured JSON/form inspection covers nested escaped strings; byte/traversal limits prevent unlimited parsing. Rust owns a request context, validates engine ownership and prevents duplicate finalization. The pure ASGI adapter preserves body replay and streaming. Finalization occurs at response start; logged duration measures time to headers, not stream completion. Response elapsed time uses a Rust monotonic clock so wall-clock adjustments do not invalidate requests. Routes and policies An unknown path is still evaluated by applicable checks; it is not automatically denied just because no route exists. Full/partial exemption decorators and required middleware supply endpoint facts. Required decorators override decorator exemptions; profile-level path/IP exemptions remain global. Native paths are literal case-insensitive prefixes, not globs. Legacy PATH_RULES, generated manifests, custom stores and uppercase settings are not imported. State and workers Policy CSVs retain shared allowlist, blocklist, keyword, geo and path schemas with native locked mutations and validated snapshots. Rate buckets default to process memory; rate_backend="csv" shares persistent buckets. UUID scores and anomaly history are per worker. Redis and custom ORM stores are unsupported in this profile. Honeypot timestamps default to shared persistent CSV with immediately synced writes. honeypot_backend="memory" uses an expiring Rust map per engine/worker; GET updates and POST evaluation/clearing avoid the durable CSV rewrite. Memory timestamps reset on restart and are not shared with other workers. Switching backend does not migrate existing timestamps. Request logs append immediately; log_fsync defaults to false and optionally syncs each row. This setting does not weaken synchronization of changed policy-state CSV writes. Training and inference Pass a trained six-feature aiwaf_rust.IsolationForest as model= in Flask/FastAPI, or set AIWAF_CSV_PIPELINE_MODEL in Django. Without a loaded model, history and eligible 404 learning continue, but model-based blocking is absent. pipeline.native.set_model(model) copies an owned snapshot; set_model(None) disables inference. Updating the original model does not change the installed snapshot. CSV/gzip training uses TrainingCSVReader , retained NativeTrainingBatch and NativeTrainingBuilder . Python still coordinates training, compatible timestamps, route discovery and artifact storage. Installing Rust does not mean the entire package has been rewritten. Source map rust/src/csv_pipeline.rs : profile, state and begin/finish enforcement. py/aiwaf/core/csv_pipeline.py : startup validation and transport facts. py/aiwaf/flask/csv_pipeline.py : Flask hooks. py/aiwaf/fast/csv_pipeline.py : pure ASGI transport. py/aiwaf/django/csv_pipeline.py : Django request/response adaptation. Continue with the request lifecycle , the native profile , migration , and performance and deployment . Legacy adapter architecture The following sections describe the existing middleware chains and compatibility interfaces. Their route manifests, settings and fallback behavior are separate from the native profile above. Shared and legacy module boundaries Source area Responsibility py/aiwaf/core/ Shared exemptions, middleware planning, route discovery, storage, reputation, training, and native capability bridges. py/aiwaf/django/ Django middleware, ORM models, decorators, settings compatibility, and management commands. py/aiwaf/flask/ Flask application initialization, request/response hooks, stores, and CLI integration. py/aiwaf/fast/ FastAPI-facing exports and middleware; the shared orchestrator lives in core/runtime_fastapi.py . Initialization and policy planning Initialization normalizes settings, selects storage, and resolves the requested middleware set. middleware_plan.py expands canonical selections and applies disabled checks. Route discovery supplies hints such as UUID routes and application intent, while path_manifest.py loads generated path policies. The resulting middleware plan determines which framework hooks are registered. A route plan then decides whether each registered protection applies to a particular request. Global enablement and per-route applicability are different questions. How each adapter executes Adapter Request boundary Response boundary Django The configured MIDDLEWARE order determines nested request execution. The unified alias expands the AIWAF stack; individual classes permit explicit ordering. The framework unwinds response handling through middleware. Logging and checks that use outcomes need to observe that response. Flask flask_integration.py registers selected middleware objects and their Flask request hooks. A returned response stops normal handler dispatch. Response hooks observe the handler result for logging and relevant behavior checks. FastAPI runtime_fastapi.py registers Starlette middleware in reverse order because the last registered wrapper executes first. Response control returns through the wrapper chain; the orchestrator coordinates configuration and lifecycle integration. FastAPI's orchestrator documents the effective available chain as Geo, IP/keyword, Rate, AI, Honeypot, UUID, Header, and Logging. Disabled or inapplicable layers are skipped. Do not infer execution order from the order of add_middleware calls alone. Following one request Resolve context Read request metadata and the resolved endpoint where available. Apply route policy Check path rules and endpoint exemption or protection metadata for each layer. Enforce selected checks Consult block state, counters, validation rules, and the available anomaly model. Observe outcome Allow the handler or return a denial, then record the response through applicable hooks. The exact shortcut behavior belongs to each middleware. An exempt path, an exempt client, a geo-only exemption, and a decorator disabling one check are distinct policies. Use the layer-specific decision to explain a bypass rather than assuming that every exemption disables the complete stack. Live routes, manifests, and decorators The CLI imports the actual application object or Django URL configuration and enumerates registered routes. Where handler source is available, static analysis adds method, API, form, and authentication signals. The generated .aiwaf/paths.json is a policy input, not a replacement router. Manifest compilation creates path rules for middleware enablement and rate overrides. Explicit decorators carry endpoint intent: aiwaf_exempt , aiwaf_exempt_from , aiwaf_only , and aiwaf_require_protection . They complement global configuration. Regenerate a manifest when live registrations change so the policy does not describe an older application. Storage and reputation The shared runtime storage layer provides memory, JSON-file, SQLite, and canonical policy CSV backends. Flask, FastAPI, Django CSV mode, and the native Rust pipeline use blacklist.csv , whitelist.csv , keywords.csv , geo_blocked_countries.csv , and path_exemptions.csv . Keyword frequencies and non-policy runtime history are stored separately in runtime_metadata.csv . Framework database modes and model storage remain separately configured. Reputation-based blocklisting stores weighted offenses, temporary-block escalation, expiration, and metadata. A later request reads that state rather than recomputing an entire traffic history. Startup imports legacy runtime key/value CSV data once, retaining original files and a completion marker. Read the shared CSV migration guide before upgrading. Memory is local to a process. Persisting an operational store does not automatically make every rate bucket or recent-request buffer distributed. FastAPI can supply a Redis-backed rate cache; review the storage semantics of the other enabled checks separately. Training and scoring Feature What it describes Why it helps path_len Length of the request path. Unusually long probing paths. kw_hits Matches against malicious keywords. Known probing patterns within a path. resp_time Response duration in seconds. Behavior that differs from the normal timing distribution. status_idx An encoded response-status category. Response outcomes without treating status codes as continuous measurements. burst_count Requests associated with the client in the burst window. Rapid repeated activity. total_404 Not-found responses in the relevant per-client history. Repeated discovery of nonexistent routes. The feature order is part of the model contract. A trainer and scorer must agree on the order, status mapping, time units, and window semantics. Summary fields ending in _ms use milliseconds; the feature vector uses seconds. Sharing feature names alone does not make every model artifact interchangeable. Request logs Completed responses supply paths, client identity, status, and timing. Feature extraction Records are normalized and combined with per-client activity windows. Train and review Volume thresholds gate model training; route exemptions filter learned keywords. Publish artifacts The runtime loads persisted model state and updated learned keywords. The training job is separate from ordinary application request handling. Reading logs and rebuilding a forest does not need to happen for every request. Runtime keyword learning, where enabled, is a separate mechanism that can use completed-response signals. The trainer parses logs, extracts behavior, filters legitimate route tokens from keyword learning, and trains only when configured volume thresholds permit. Request-time scoring reads an available model; lack of a usable model does not remove deterministic header, rate, keyword, or geo controls. Model artifacts carry forest state and metadata in JSON. Current Python persistence does not load pickle or joblib objects. That serialization boundary is separate from the choice of file, database, or cache for storing the artifact. The Rust acceleration boundary In legacy adapters, rust_backend.py discovers installed aiwaf_rust capabilities. Supported native operations accelerate matching, header validation, feature extraction, and forest operations while the Python adapter owns request/response dispatch. Python 1.1.4 declares the Rust package as a required installation dependency. The compatibility bridge normalizes HTTP and WSGI header names and retains guarded Python paths for custom integrations or unavailable legacy capabilities. The explicit CSVPipeline instead requires NativeCSVPipeline at startup and keeps its enforcement core in Rust; it does not use a Python policy fallback. These are separate execution choices. Worked example: an API request and a scanner A JSON API handler can carry route metadata that omits HTML form timing. Header and rate checks still apply when selected. Allowed requests reach the handler, and the logger records its actual result. A scanner requesting many missing paths creates a different record: suspicious keyword hits, repeated 404s, and burst activity. Keyword or rate checks may reject it immediately. Sufficient logs later give the trainer behavior data for the anomaly path. Each decision should be explainable by its enabled layer and recorded reason. System overview connects these components. The setup guides show wiring, and operations covers migration and training commands. Trace the implementation Follow these files in the monorepo to connect the architecture to the code: py/aiwaf/core/middleware_plan.py py/aiwaf/core/path_manifest.py py/aiwaf/core/runtime_fastapi.py py/aiwaf/flask/flask_integration.py py/aiwaf/django/middleware.py py/aiwaf/core/runtime_blocklist.py py/aiwaf/core/rust_backend.py Shared Python CSV storage List APIs and command help now use blocklist and allowlist . Earlier import/method/command spellings remain compatibility aliases. Existing CSV filenames and Django model identity are retained so upgrades preserve stored blocks and exemptions; use the package storage constants rather than constructing filenames. Python 1.1.4 standardizes Flask, FastAPI, Django CSV mode, and the explicit native pipeline on blacklist.csv , whitelist.csv , keywords.csv , geo_blocked_countries.csv , and path_exemptions.csv . Keyword frequencies and non-policy runtime history are retained in runtime_metadata.csv . Memory, JSON-file, database, and Django ORM modes keep their existing storage behavior. Integration CSV directory configuration Legacy Flask Set app.config['AIWAF_USE_CSV'] = True and app.config['AIWAF_DATA_DIR'] before initializing AIWAF. Legacy Django Set AIWAF_STORAGE_MODE = "csv" and AIWAF_DATA_DIR in project settings. Legacy FastAPI Pass storage={"backend": "csv", "data_dir": "/absolute/path/aiwaf_data"} to AIWAF . Its default backend remains memory. Native adapters Pass the lowercase data_dir in the dedicated native profile. Native adapters do not inherit legacy framework settings. Startup imports legacy runtime CSV data once, preserving block expiry and metadata. Original sources remain intact; backups and completion markers support recovery and prevent removed entries from returning on restart. Existing canonical policy wins conflicts. Stop old workers before upgrading and use the same absolute directory for the application and CLI. See migration paths and recovery . Flask management searches existing project aiwaf_data and .aiwaf/data before user/package directories. Explicit AIWAF_DATA_DIR or --data-dir takes priority. The five policy files use UTF-8 across Python and Rust. Sharing these files does not make memory rate buckets, model history, or optional memory form timing distributed. Flask and FastAPI native honeypot cache Python 1.1.8 with aiwaf-rust 0.2.7 adds opt-in Redis and supplied-cache timing to both native adapters. CSV remains their default. Rust retains timing rules and exemptions; only timestamp I/O uses the cache. import os profile = { "data_dir": "aiwaf_data", "honeypot_backend": "redis", "honeypot_redis_url": os.environ["AIWAF_REDIS_URL"], "honeypot_cache_namespace": "myapp:honeypot:v1", } # Flask: from aiwaf.flask.csv_pipeline import NativeAIWAF NativeAIWAF(app, config=profile) # FastAPI alternative: # from aiwaf.fast.csv_pipeline import NativeAIWAFMiddleware # app.add_middleware(NativeAIWAFMiddleware, config=profile) For Flask-Caching or a compatible custom object, use honeypot_backend="cache" and pass honeypot_cache=cache to the native adapter. It must provide synchronous get(key) and set(key, value, timeout=seconds) , preserve the timestamp/expiry pair, honor TTL and propagate errors. A false write result means failure; silent/no-op backends are unsuitable. Local caches remain worker-local. Use a shared backend and the same namespace across workers; isolate unrelated applications with different namespaces. Records have a 300-second TTL. Missing/evicted timestamps allow the timing check, while cache errors and invalid records return generic HTTP 503. Expired-page POSTs return 409 until a new GET or TTL expiry; old snapshots are not deleted. FastAPI runs cache-backed native checks in its worker thread pool so synchronous cache I/O does not block the event loop. Other policy stores and legacy middleware behavior are unchanged. Django native honeypot cache Python 1.1.8 with aiwaf-rust 0.2.7 defaults Django native honeypot timing to Django's configured cache. Set honeypot_cache_alias in AIWAF_CSV_PIPELINE to select an alias; it defaults to default . Rust calls a small Python cache adapter for timestamp I/O and retains timing decisions, logical expiry and exemptions. Other policy CSVs and rate-limit configuration are unchanged. AIWAF_CSV_PIPELINE = { "data_dir": "aiwaf_data", "honeypot_cache_alias": "default", } # Configure CACHES["default"] with a shared backend for multiple workers. Redis or Memcached can share timestamps across workers. LocMemCache is supported with a startup warning; it remains worker-local. DummyCache is rejected when honeypot protection is enabled. Cache errors, failed writes and invalid records produce generic HTTP 503; known ignored-cache-error modes are rejected. Entries use a 300-second TTL. Expired-page POSTs return 409 until a new GET or TTL expiry. No eager deletion occurs, so an old POST cannot erase a concurrent refresh. A missing or evicted timestamp allows the POST timing check, as before; cache failure is not treated as a miss. Backends do not transfer existing timestamps. Install the matching Rust extension and restart workers together. Explicit honeypot_backend="csv" retains filesystem timing; "memory" uses Rust's per-engine map. Flask, FastAPI and direct native construction keep CSV as the default. See the Django cache documentation . Training replay protection Python 1.1.6 with aiwaf-rust 0.2.5 uses Rust-owned receipts in Flask, FastAPI, and Django. Reusing requests already handled by training cannot extend or recreate a block. Fresh requests must independently satisfy enforcement rules; models and keyword learning can still reuse historical logs. Keep training_evidence.json across expiry, manual unblocking, log rotation, and restarts. It lives in the policy data directory unless AIWAF_TRAINING_STATE_DIR selects another durable directory. Trainers sharing a blocklist must share that directory. Receipts start with this release and cannot reconstruct decisions made by older versions. Missing native support and corrupt state stop training visibly. Block and receipt writes are separate, so a crash between them can require recovery. Flask CLI listing now filters expired entries without rewriting an older snapshot over blocks concurrently added or refreshed by a trainer. The CLI displays the canonical added_date , with the older timestamp as a fallback. This listing fix and training replay protection address different causes of block changes. A first temporary block defaults to 900 seconds; later reputation decisions can increase its duration. Check the stored expiry rather than assuming every block lasts 24 hours.

title: Python Operations and Migration
text: Python Operations and Migration How AIWAF works: system architecture Unified CLI # Bare help selects the single installed framework aiwaf --help # Explicit Flask policy commands aiwaf flask blocklist migrate aiwaf flask status # Django management commands python manage.py detect_and_train python manage.py regenerate_model python manage.py aiwaf_reset --keywords --confirm python manage.py aiwaf_logging --status python manage.py geo_block_country list # Explicit adapter dispatch aiwaf django aiwaf_list --all aiwaf flask --help aiwaf fastapi --help Bare commands select the single installed supported framework. When several frameworks are installed, use an explicit prefix: aiwaf flask ... , aiwaf fastapi ... , or aiwaf django <management-command> ... . fast remains a FastAPI alias. aiwaf init accepts --framework and --app for route discovery; these flags do not choose the adapter for bare commands. FastAPI training has its own --app option. Django uses its management-command names; bare status is not a Django management command. Blocklist migration Version 1.0.7 introduced weighted reputation, progressively longer temporary blocks, expiration, and richer blocklist metadata. Existing blocklist data has compatibility handling; aiwaf blocklist migrate performs backend-aware migration. Legacy CSV schemas are detected and imported permanent blocks are converted safely. Review existing entries and back up runtime state before migration. Model storage Persisted Python models use JSON state. Pickle, joblib, and executable Python-object formats are unsupported. Regenerate old model artifacts through the current trainer. Python 1.1.8 installs its required aiwaf-rust>=0.2.7 dependency. Legacy adapters select supported native operations while retaining their compatibility paths; the complete native pipeline requires an explicit adapter and has no Python policy fallback. Local development and verification Run from the monorepo root: python -m pip install -e ".[django,flask,fastapi,rust]" python -m pip install pytest pytest-cov coverage httpx npm ci --prefix js python aiwaf_test.py --python-only pytest python -m benchmarks.benchmark_auto_middleware Independent releases The table lists source release targets, not registry availability. Python 1.1.8 and Rust/Python 0.2.7 are local source targets; registry publication is independent. Release versions and tags must match the relevant manifest. Package Manifest Tag Workflow Python aiwaf pyproject.toml python-v1.1.8 python-publish.yml npm aiwaf js/package.json js-v1.1.5 npm-publish.yml PyPI aiwaf-rust rust/pyproject.toml + rust/Cargo.toml rust-v0.2.7 rust-publish.yml npm aiwaf-wasm rust/crates/aiwaf_wasm/Cargo.toml wasm-v0.2.5 wasm-publish.yml Maven aiwaf-java java/pom.xml java-v1.3.5 java-publish.yml Python and Rust publish to PyPI with trusted publishing. The npm workflows use npm trusted publishing and stage packages for approval. Configure the trusted publisher with organization aiwaf-project , repository aiwaf , the exact workflow filename, and the environment used by that workflow. Java publishing uses the protected maven-publish environment plus GPG_PRIVATE_KEY , GPG_PASSPHRASE , CENTRAL_TOKEN_USERNAME , and CENTRAL_TOKEN_PASSWORD . The workflow verifies the tag, runs tests, signs the POM and all three JARs, uploads the deployment bundle, and waits for Maven Central publication. Registry releases are immutable. Increment the relevant manifest version before publishing another release. Deployment Configure the application to trust forwarding headers only from known proxy CIDRs. Configure the outermost proxy to overwrite client-supplied forwarding headers. Use Redis, a database, or another shared backend when multiple workers must share rate-limit, blocklist, or exemption state. Keep health checks, static assets, and trusted webhook routes explicitly scoped instead of disabling protection globally. Start anomaly detection in observe-only or conservative mode and tune it with representative normal traffic. Rotate logs and exclude secrets, authorization headers, cookies, and personal data. Sign model/configuration artifacts where the runtime supports HMAC verification. Run AIWAF alongside normal secure-development controls and an edge/reverse-proxy layer. Rust-backed CSV operations and training Python 1.1.8 requires aiwaf-rust>=0.2.7 as a base dependency. Framework extras select Django, Flask or FastAPI. The optional rust extra remains an installation alias. Legacy capability selection is automatic unless disabled; the new complete pipeline requires the explicit adapter. pip install "aiwaf[flask,rust]" # Run these repository scripts with the matching installed packages. python scripts/check_native_csv_runtime.py python scripts/check_csv_release_concurrency.py # FastAPI: import the live application and use its routes/runtime stores. aiwaf fastapi train --app app:app --log-dir aiwaf_logs --disable-ai aiwaf fastapi train --app app:app --log-dir aiwaf_logs --model-path model.json # Django retains its management-command workflow. python manage.py detect_and_train FastAPI also exposes aiwaf.fast.trainer.train_from_logs(app, ...) . --data-dir selects the shared policy CSV directory and imports an existing legacy runtime_store.csv once. Training writes shared keyword and blocklist files; keyword frequencies are retained in auxiliary runtime metadata. AI training obeys its volume threshold; --force-ai explicitly overrides that threshold. Training optionally writes a JSON model artifact. Reload the model explicitly or restart the application: existing FastAPI anomaly middleware instances do not automatically adopt the new forest. Flask, Django CSV, and FastAPI stream plain/gzip CSV directly in bounded batches, including quoted newlines and seconds/milliseconds timing fields. Supported Apache logs use batched extraction and timestamp parsing. Django preserves its legacy CSV timezone/microsecond truncation; Flask and FastAPI preserve ISO offsets. Unique route checks, per-IP aggregation, and keyword persistence are batched. Native feature handles keep the matrix, forest fitting/prediction, and anomaly statistics in Rust, without a Pandas DataFrame. Custom parsers, missing capabilities, and Unicode keyword learning retain compatibility paths. CSV access logs are written and flushed synchronously under OS locks. Cached writer handles detect rotation, replacement, and truncation. After requests stop, call the Flask logger's close() or aiwaf.core.native_runtime.close_csv_logs() before deleting temporary directories, especially on Windows. Handles also close at process shutdown. AIWAF_CSV_LOG_FSYNC=True adds per-row disk sync; without it, a system crash can lose recently flushed OS-buffered entries. There is no application-side logging queue. Native pipeline performance and deployment Release candidate: this page documents Python 1.1.8 and Rust/Python 0.2.7 in the current source checkout. Source versions do not establish registry availability. Python 1.1.8 requires aiwaf-rust>=0.2.7 ; framework dependencies remain extras. Matched WSL Linux measurements used all eight stages, immediate CSV logging, 1,000 blocklist entries, 80% GET / 20% JSON POST (30 fields), and one concurrent client. Three alternating 300-request runs per framework/mode used a seeded 100-tree Rust forest and 200 initial history records per client when AI was enabled. GeoIP reflects a local fixture. Framework CSV timing, AI off Memory timing, AI off CSV timing, AI on Memory timing, AI on Flask 3.74 ms 0.83 ms 3.66 ms 0.97 ms Django 3.67 ms 0.91 ms 4.02 ms 0.83 ms FastAPI 3.78 ms 0.78 ms 3.70 ms 0.92 ms These are added server processing latency : median of per-run mean protected times minus the corresponding framework-only baseline. They are not total request latency, network latency or production throughput. Memory reduced measured overhead by 73–79% versus persistent CSV timing, with different persistence and worker-sharing semantics. All 13,500 measured requests returned 200; protected PHP/SQL probes returned 403. Reproduce from the monorepo with scripts/benchmark_release_http.py --pipeline ; add --honeypot-backend memory for memory mode. Include a framework-only baseline using the same handler, workload and server. Compare your production filesystem, worker count and real GeoIP/model workload before setting latency expectations. Model and worker lifecycle Pass a trained Rust IsolationForest as model= , or use Django's AIWAF_CSV_PIPELINE_MODEL . Load a new snapshot with pipeline.native.set_model(model) where you hold the engine reference, or reload workers. Native initialization does not automatically train or load the legacy adapter's model artifact. The runtime's diagnostics() reports model activation and state counts. Release order Publish aiwaf-rust 0.2.7 before aiwaf 1.1.8 . Native wheels target Linux x86_64/aarch64, musl x86_64, macOS x86_64/arm64 and Windows x86_64. Windows and WSL builds were checked locally; all remaining wheel targets must pass release CI. Local validation passed eight test groups and ten independent Windows native API smoke checks. These local checks do not replace platform CI. Continue with the request lifecycle , the native profile , migration , and performance and deployment . Python 1.1.4 CSV migration checks (historical) This source release adds installed-framework CLI detection, the explicit fastapi alias, reuse of existing Flask data directories, and shared policy CSV startup migration. Local validation passed a broad 869-test core/Flask/FastAPI run, 284 tests through Django's test runner, and focused migration/UTF-8 compatibility checks. The 1.1.4 wheel and source archive were built and the packaged version, CSV backend, and required Rust dependency were verified. Source artifacts do not establish that a registry release has been published. The benchmark tables on this page predate the 1.1.4 migration changes. Rerun the same baseline-subtracted benchmark for the deployed version and filesystem. October 2026 release upgrade The prepared source versions are Python 1.1.6 , Rust/Python 0.2.5 , Node.js 1.1.4 , WASM 0.2.4 , and Java 1.3.4 . Node offline training requires the matching WASM receipt API. Back up policies, logs, models, and training evidence. Use the same absolute data and evidence directories for application workers and CLI trainers. Install the matching native companion before upgrading its host package: Rust before Python, WASM before Node. Preserve training_evidence.json and node_training_evidence.json across expiry, unblocking, restarts, and log rotation. Stop older file writers and restart all workers on the new code. Add genuinely fresh requests and confirm they must independently satisfy the enforcement threshold. Verify that listing and expiry checks preserve concurrently refreshed blocks and unrelated IPs. Check the raw expiry and backend location if entries disappear unexpectedly. Java CSV and file storage Java 1.3.4 reloads current storage under a shared JVM and OS sidecar lock for each operation. Reads filter expiry without rewriting disk; mutations preserve other instances' updates and report persistence failures. This adds file I/O. Java model training still does not add blocklist entries. Rate buckets and other per-engine memory state retain their existing isolation. Lock recovery Python training uses an OS file lock; Java CSV/file OS locks also release on process exit. Keep their stable sidecar lock files in place while workers run. Node uses lock directories for training and legacy CSV mutations; a crash can leave them behind. Confirm the owning process has stopped before removing a Node lock directory. Do not delete training receipts to clear a lock: doing so loses handled-evidence history. Release checks Local validation passed 247 Node tests across 67 suites with the coverage gate, 215 Java tests with 3 skips, and 38 Rust/WASM native tests. After the native dependency bump, 11 affected Python packaging tests passed through the appropriate Django and pytest runners. These checks do not replace full release CI, dependency audits, signing, or operating-system wheel builds. Build Linux/macOS Rust wheels using the release matrix; the local bundle contains a Windows x86-64 wheel. For release maintainers: publish the WASM companion, refresh the Node lockfile from the registry to record its actual integrity, then run npm ci and the native integration checks. Do not substitute an older native dependency to satisfy a stale packaging test. See the changelog .

title: Django Setup
text: Django Setup Release candidate: this page documents Python 1.1.8 and Rust/Python 0.2.7 in the current source checkout. Source versions do not establish registry availability. Python 1.1.8 requires aiwaf-rust>=0.2.7 ; framework dependencies remain extras. This guide retains the legacy integration steps. Use the native adapter example for the Rust-owned CSV pipeline. How AIWAF works: system architecture Add AIWAF to a Django application and verify that protection is registered with the live route table. Before you begin Use an environment compatible with your framework. This guide assumes an existing Django project with manage.py and a settings module. New to middleware? Start with the six-step first protected app tutorial , which includes complete files and expected responses. 1. Install the framework extra pip install "aiwaf[django]" # Python 1.1.4 installs its required Rust runtime automatically. Install into the environment used to run your application. Choose an interpreter compatible with the framework and dependencies. 2. Register protection project/settings.py (merge into existing lists) Add the app and the unified middleware alias in settings.py : INSTALLED_APPS = [ # ... Stop old workers before upgrading and use the same absolute directory for the application and CLI. See migration paths and recovery . Flask management searches existing project aiwaf_data and .aiwaf/data before user/package directories. Explicit AIWAF_DATA_DIR or --data-dir takes priority. The five policy files use UTF-8 across Python and Rust. Sharing these files does not make memory rate buckets, model history, or optional memory form timing distributed. Flask and FastAPI native honeypot cache Python 1.1.8 with aiwaf-rust 0.2.7 adds opt-in Redis and supplied-cache timing to both native adapters. CSV remains their default. Rust retains timing rules and exemptions; only timestamp I/O uses the cache. import os profile = { "data_dir": "aiwaf_data", "honeypot_backend": "redis", "honeypot_redis_url": os.environ["AIWAF_REDIS_URL"], "honeypot_cache_namespace": "myapp:honeypot:v1", } # Flask: from aiwaf.flask.csv_pipeline import NativeAIWAF NativeAIWAF(app, config=profile) # FastAPI alternative: # from aiwaf.fast.csv_pipeline import NativeAIWAFMiddleware # app.add_middleware(NativeAIWAFMiddleware, config=profile) For Flask-Caching or a compatible custom object, use honeypot_backend="cache" and pass honeypot_cache=cache to the native adapter. It must provide synchronous get(key) and set(key, value, timeout=seconds) , preserve the timestamp/expiry pair, honor TTL and propagate errors. A false write result means failure; silent/no-op backends are unsuitable. Local caches remain worker-local. Use a shared backend and the same namespace across workers; isolate unrelated applications with different namespaces. Records have a 300-second TTL. Missing/evicted timestamps allow the timing check, while cache errors and invalid records return generic HTTP 503. Expired-page POSTs return 409 until a new GET or TTL expiry; old snapshots are not deleted. FastAPI runs cache-backed native checks in its worker thread pool so synchronous cache I/O does not block the event loop. Other policy stores and legacy middleware behavior are unchanged. Django native honeypot cache Python 1.1.8 with aiwaf-rust 0.2.7 defaults Django native honeypot timing to Django's configured cache. Set honeypot_cache_alias in AIWAF_CSV_PIPELINE to select an alias; it defaults to default . Rust calls a small Python cache adapter for timestamp I/O and retains timing decisions, logical expiry and exemptions. Other policy CSVs and rate-limit configuration are unchanged. AIWAF_CSV_PIPELINE = { "data_dir": "aiwaf_data", "honeypot_cache_alias": "default", } # Configure CACHES["default"] with a shared backend for multiple workers. Redis or Memcached can share timestamps across workers. LocMemCache is supported with a startup warning; it remains worker-local. DummyCache is rejected when honeypot protection is enabled. Cache errors, failed writes and invalid records produce generic HTTP 503; known ignored-cache-error modes are rejected. Entries use a 300-second TTL. Expired-page POSTs return 409 until a new GET or TTL expiry. No eager deletion occurs, so an old POST cannot erase a concurrent refresh. A missing or evicted timestamp allows the POST timing check, as before; cache failure is not treated as a miss. Backends do not transfer existing timestamps. Install the matching Rust extension and restart workers together. Explicit honeypot_backend="csv" retains filesystem timing; "memory" uses Rust's per-engine map. Flask, FastAPI and direct native construction keep CSV as the default. See the Django cache documentation . Training replay protection Python 1.1.6 with aiwaf-rust 0.2.5 uses Rust-owned receipts in Flask, FastAPI, and Django. Reusing requests already handled by training cannot extend or recreate a block. Fresh requests must independently satisfy enforcement rules; models and keyword learning can still reuse historical logs. Keep training_evidence.json across expiry, manual unblocking, log rotation, and restarts. It lives in the policy data directory unless AIWAF_TRAINING_STATE_DIR selects another durable directory. Trainers sharing a blocklist must share that directory. Receipts start with this release and cannot reconstruct decisions made by older versions. Missing native support and corrupt state stop training visibly. Block and receipt writes are separate, so a crash between them can require recovery. Flask CLI listing now filters expired entries without rewriting an older snapshot over blocks concurrently added or refreshed by a trainer. The CLI displays the canonical added_date , with the older timestamp as a fallback. This listing fix and training replay protection address different causes of block changes. A first temporary block defaults to 900 seconds; later reputation decisions can increase its duration. Check the stored expiry rather than assuming every block lasts 24 hours.

title: Rust and WebAssembly Accelerators
text: Rust and WebAssembly Accelerators How AIWAF works: system architecture aiwaf-rust and aiwaf-wasm are versioned independently from the Python and Node packages. The Rust/Python source release candidate is 0.2.3 ; WASM remains 0.2.2 . They share rust/crates/aiwaf_core/ ; PyO3 bindings live in rust/src/lib.rs , and WASM bindings in rust/crates/aiwaf_wasm/ . Python bindings aiwaf-rust exposes the shared Rust core through PyO3 and ABI3 wheels for Python 3.8 and newer. pip install aiwaf-rust The module provides: validate_headers and validate_headers_with_config KeywordMatcher and RouteMatcher request-record construction and six-feature extraction incremental feature extraction with explicit state recent-behavior analysis IsolationForest training, scoring, prediction, retraining, and JSON state import aiwaf_rust reason = aiwaf_rust.validate_headers({ "HTTP_USER_AGENT": "Mozilla/5.0", "HTTP_ACCEPT": "text/html", }) forest = aiwaf_rust.IsolationForest( n_estimators=100, max_samples="auto", contamination="auto", max_features=1.0, bootstrap=False, random_state=42, warm_start=False, ) forest.fit([[0.1, 1.0], [0.2, 1.1], [9.0, 9.0]]) score = forest.anomaly_score([9.0, 9.0]) state = forest.to_json() restored = aiwaf_rust.IsolationForest.from_json(state) For a local native build, stage the two canonical repository assets and run maturin: cp README.md rust/README.md cp LICENSE rust/LICENSE cp NOTICE rust/NOTICE cp -R licenses rust/ python -m pip install maturin cd rust maturin develop The staged files are ignored by Git. Release automation performs the same staging before building wheels and the source distribution. WebAssembly bindings aiwaf-wasm exposes the shared Rust core to browsers and Node-compatible bundlers. import init, { IsolationForest, KeywordMatcher, RouteMatcher, analyze_recent_behavior, extract_features, validate_headers, } from 'aiwaf-wasm'; await init(); const reason = validate_headers({ 'user-agent': 'Mozilla/5.0', accept: 'text/html' }); const forest = new IsolationForest({ n_estimators: 100, max_samples: 'auto', contamination: 'auto', random_state: 42 }); forest.fit([[0.1, 1.0], [0.2, 1.1], [9.0, 9.0]]); const score = forest.anomaly_score([9.0, 9.0]); The WASM API includes header, URL, and content validation; keyword and route matchers; record conversion; batched feature extraction; recent-behavior analysis; and Isolation Forest lifecycle methods. Browser use requires a bundler that understands WebAssembly assets. Build and test it locally: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --locked -p aiwaf_core cd rust/crates/aiwaf_wasm wasm-pack test --node wasm-pack build --release --target bundler cd ../.. python scripts/patch_wasm_pkg.py cp ../LICENSE crates/aiwaf_wasm/pkg/LICENSE cp ../NOTICE crates/aiwaf_wasm/pkg/NOTICE cp -R ../licenses crates/aiwaf_wasm/pkg/ Continue Binding API and scoring semantics Build, tests, and packaging Native CSV request engine and training Release candidate: this page documents Python 1.1.8 and Rust/Python 0.2.7 in the current source checkout. Source versions do not establish registry availability. Python 1.1.8 requires aiwaf-rust>=0.2.7 ; framework dependencies remain extras. Rust owns the native CSV pipeline configuration, enforcement order, SQL and keyword inspection, geo/blocklist decisions, rate buckets, form timing, UUID scores, anomaly history/inference, keyword learning, and CSV logging. Python supplies framework routes, authentication facts, GeoIP lookup, bounded request buffering, and response construction. Training and management still have Python interfaces. PyO3 exposes NativeCSVPipeline and opaque NativePipelineRequest , alongside locked CSV transactions, snapshots, cached append writers, TrainingCSVReader , NativeTrainingBatch and NativeTrainingBuilder . Native ISO parsing remains optional in compatibility training paths. WASM has a separate API: it does not expose this filesystem request pipeline or retained Python training objects. Continue with the request lifecycle , the native profile , migration , and performance and deployment .

title: Rust and WASM Architecture
text: Rust and WASM Architecture Rust implements shared computation primitives. PyO3 and wasm-bindgen expose them to host applications, while the host owns framework hooks and responses. Python PyO3 bindings also provide native CSV storage, logging writes, and shared policy computations; the WASM filesystem boundary remains different. On this page One core, two binding boundaries Matching without rebuilding work per request Record conversion and stateful feature extraction Inside the forest JSON is the artifact boundary Acceleration has a conversion cost Worked example: accelerated header validation Trace the implementation How AIWAF works: system architecture One core, two binding boundaries Host runtime Select the operation and provide normalized input. Binding conversion PyO3 or wasm-bindgen converts host values into Rust data. Shared Rust core Match, validate, extract features, analyze behavior, or score a forest. Host decision Convert the result back and apply framework policy. Source area Responsibility rust/crates/aiwaf_core/src/lib.rs Shared keyword and route matching, request records, feature windows, behavior analysis, and Isolation Forest state. rust/src/lib.rs PyO3 objects and conversion routines exposed as aiwaf_rust . rust/crates/aiwaf_wasm/src/lib.rs wasm-bindgen exports and JavaScript conversion exposed as aiwaf-wasm . Matching without rebuilding work per request KeywordMatcher escapes configured keywords into literal patterns and builds a regex set. first_match preserves configured keyword order. The host can reuse the matcher rather than rebuilding pattern machinery on each request. RouteMatcher indexes normalized prefixes. Matching starts with the deepest candidate and walks parent path boundaries until it finds a stored prefix. Duplicate normalized prefixes retain their first configured index. The host still normalizes paths and interprets the matching rule's policy. Record conversion and stateful feature extraction Bindings convert request records into typed structures before the core computes features. Batched and incremental extraction share the computation layer; incremental calls carry explicit state so recent client activity is available across batches. That extraction state is distinct from a framework's blocklist or distributed rate-limit store. Sending a batch to Rust does not automatically replicate application state across workers. The host chooses where records and extraction state live. Feature What it describes Why it helps path_len Length of the request path. Unusually long probing paths. kw_hits Matches against malicious keywords. Known probing patterns within a path. resp_time Response duration in seconds. Behavior that differs from the normal timing distribution. status_idx An encoded response-status category. Response outcomes without treating status codes as continuous measurements. burst_count Requests associated with the client in the burst window. Rapid repeated activity. total_404 Not-found responses in the relevant per-client history. Repeated discovery of nonexistent routes. The feature order is part of the model contract. A trainer and scorer must agree on the order, status mapping, time units, and window semantics. Summary fields ending in _ms use milliseconds; the feature vector uses seconds. Sharing feature names alone does not make every model artifact interchangeable. Inside the forest Training samples rows and grows isolation trees with random feature selections and split points. Tree traversal measures the number of splits required to isolate a point; short average isolation paths indicate more unusual samples. anomaly_score uses the direction where higher means more anomalous. score_samples uses the opposite, scikit-learn-aligned direction. decision_function subtracts the configured offset, and predict returns inlier or outlier labels. The host must use the matching threshold convention. Ordinary fitting replaces the forest unless warm-start append is selected. Retraining supports the append lifecycle. Random seeds and sampling settings affect the trained state, so score comparisons should use compatible artifacts and settings. JSON is the artifact boundary The forest exports state through to_json and restores it through from_json . Tree structure, settings, and scoring state travel as data. The host decides whether to store that state in a file, database, or cache and checks feature and artifact compatibility when loading. Python's Rust-model artifact can be exchanged with the supported Java JSON model path. JavaScript-native forests and older artifacts are not automatically the same format just because they use six feature names. Acceleration has a conversion cost Python calls cross the native-extension boundary; JavaScript calls cross the WASM boundary. Converting object-heavy inputs consumes time before the Rust computation starts. Reusing matchers and processing sufficiently large feature batches can amortize that cost. The legacy Python bridge selects capabilities and retains fallback behavior. The explicit NativeCSVPipeline validates its API once and has no Python policy fallback. The Node adapter can choose JavaScript when WASM initialization or conversion is unsuitable. A native function returning a suspicious reason still requires the host to turn that result into a policy decision. Worked example: accelerated header validation The Python adapter receives framework headers and normalizes HTTP or WSGI key names. The bridge passes the resulting dictionary and validation options through PyO3. Rust evaluates the configured header rules and returns a reason or a clean result. The Python middleware then decides whether to return a response, record an offense, or continue to the handler. The Rust core never sends the Flask or FastAPI response itself. This boundary explains why framework configuration and exemptions continue to matter when native acceleration is enabled. System overview Binding API and scoring semantics Build and packaging Trace the implementation Follow these files in the monorepo to connect the architecture to the code: rust/crates/aiwaf_core/src/lib.rs rust/src/lib.rs rust/crates/aiwaf_wasm/src/lib.rs py/aiwaf/core/rust_backend.py js/lib/wasmAdapter.js Native CSV request engine and training Release candidate: this page documents Python 1.1.8 and Rust/Python 0.2.7 in the current source checkout. Source versions do not establish registry availability. Python 1.1.8 requires aiwaf-rust>=0.2.7 ; framework dependencies remain extras. Rust owns the native CSV pipeline configuration, enforcement order, SQL and keyword inspection, geo/blocklist decisions, rate buckets, form timing, UUID scores, anomaly history/inference, keyword learning, and CSV logging. Python supplies framework routes, authentication facts, GeoIP lookup, bounded request buffering, and response construction. Training and management still have Python interfaces. PyO3 exposes NativeCSVPipeline and opaque NativePipelineRequest , alongside locked CSV transactions, snapshots, cached append writers, TrainingCSVReader , NativeTrainingBatch and NativeTrainingBuilder . Native ISO parsing remains optional in compatibility training paths. WASM has a separate API: it does not expose this filesystem request pipeline or retained Python training objects.
