title: Create your first protected app
text: First protected app / Step 2 of 6 Create your first protected app In the directory you prepared, create a file named app.py . This is a complete application. You can copy the whole block without filling in missing routes or configuration. 1. Create app.py app.py """Local learning app. Its small limits are for the tutorial, not production.""" from flask import Flask from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF, aiwaf_exempt app = Flask(__name__) app.config.update( AIWAF_USE_CSV=True, AIWAF_DATA_DIR="aiwaf_data", AIWAF_RATE_WINDOW=60, AIWAF_RATE_MAX=3, AIWAF_RATE_FLOOD=100, AIWAF_PATH_RULES=[ {"PREFIX": "/api/message", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}}, ], AIWAF_LOG_DIR="aiwaf_logs", AIWAF_LOG_FORMAT="json", ) @app.get("/api/message") def message(): return {"message": "Hello from a protected route"} @app.get("/health") @aiwaf_exempt def health(): return {"ok": True} AIWAF(app, middlewares=["rate_limit", "logging"]) 2. Understand the pieces Flask(__name__) creates the application object. It is named app , so both Flask and the AIWAF CLI will use the import target app:app . app.config.update(...) applies settings before middleware registration. The teaching limit is three requests in 60 seconds; the flood threshold is intentionally higher so the rate-limit demonstration does not create a flood block. AIWAF_PATH_RULES pins the message route to the teaching budget. Generated manifests can supply inferred rate settings; the explicit rule keeps this exercise at three requests. /api/message is the protected route. The handler runs only when the selected middleware allows the request. @aiwaf_exempt marks /health as exempt from protection. Use this deliberately for liveness; it does not turn off checks for other routes. AIWAF(...) registers rate limiting and logging after the routes have been defined. Header, keyword, geo, and anomaly checks are not selected in this teaching app, making the first verification predictable with a plain HTTP client. Selected checks are a learning choice The app demonstrates two components. It is not a complete production security policy. The framework setup and architecture guides explain all , auto , and the other checks. 3. Start the development server python -m flask --app app:app run --port 5000 The console should report a development server listening at http://127.0.0.1:5000 . Leave that terminal open. Flask's development server is suitable for this local exercise; choose your framework's production server before deployment. 4. Recognize the generated files aiwaf-demo/ app.py .venv/ aiwaf_logs/ # request logs aiwaf_data/ # CSV state when a store needs it .aiwaf/ # route manifest after the next step Runtime directories are created as they are needed. Keep the application source in Git; ignore the virtual environment, request logs, local state, and generated route manifest. Checkpoint Your server starts from app.py without Redis or a trained anomaly model. Do not send repeated requests yet; the verification chapter starts with a fresh counter. Previous: Prepare your environment Next: Discover your routes

title: Prepare your environment
text: First protected app / Step 1 of 6 Prepare your environment This tutorial builds a small Flask API and follows one request from the client through AIWAF to the handler and request log. You will see three successful requests followed by a rate-limit response, and then exempt one route without removing protection from the others. Before you begin Use Python 3.11 or newer, a terminal, and an empty directory. The commands use the current Python AIWAF API. They do not require Redis, a trained model, or the AIWAF source checkout. Python 1.1.4 installs the required Rust runtime. Flask is the teaching example; use the framework guides if you are integrating an existing app. 1. Create a workspace mkdir aiwaf-demo cd aiwaf-demo python -m venv .venv A virtual environment keeps the tutorial's packages separate from other applications. Run every later command from this directory with that environment active. 2. Activate the environment Linux and macOS source .venv/bin/activate Windows PowerShell .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 If your machine names Python python3 or uses the py launcher, use that command to create the environment. Once active, python should refer to its interpreter. 3. Install the framework extra python -m pip install "aiwaf[flask]" python -m pip show aiwaf Flask The flask extra installs the dependencies for the Flask adapter. Python 1.1.4 also installs aiwaf-rust>=0.2.3 . This walkthrough uses the legacy Flask adapter; the complete native pipeline is configured with NativeAIWAF . 4. Check the import python -c "from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF; print('Flask adapter ready')" Flask adapter ready If the import fails, compare python -m pip --version with the active interpreter. Do not install packages into a different environment to silence the error. Checkpoint You have an isolated environment and can import the Flask adapter. No server or model is running yet. Previous: Choose a runtime Next: Create your first protected app

title: Read logs and plan training
text: First protected app / Step 6 of 6 Read logs and plan training Enforcement decisions are easier to operate when you can connect them to request observations. The tutorial already selects logging; now inspect the files it writes and understand the boundary between logging and training. 1. Read the access log From the app directory: python -c "from pathlib import Path; print(Path('aiwaf_logs/access.log').read_text())" AIWAF_LOG_FORMAT='json' writes JSON records to the access log. Look for the request path and response status for the message/preview calls. Timestamps, durations, addresses, and record details depend on the runtime; the file is evidence of the observed requests, not a trained model. 2. Separate three kinds of state Data Purpose Tutorial behavior Rate counters Decide whether the current request crosses the window In memory in this process; lost on restart Request logs / CSV state Record observations and persist store data when used Files under the configured directories Model artifact Score behavior after offline training No anomaly model is trained or selected here Keeping CSV files does not make rate counters shared across workers. See shared state configuration before scaling beyond a single process. 3. Inspect the trainer before running it aiwaf flask train --help aiwaf flask model --help For an application with a representative combined-format log corpus, the Flask trainer accepts: aiwaf flask train --log-dir /path/to/combined-format-logs This is a separate operational example, not the next command to run on these few JSON tutorial records. Check the installed trainer's supported input formats, volume thresholds, output path, and model diagnostics. Convert or collect a supported log format deliberately; do not assume the logger format is the trainer format. Current Python persisted models use JSON. A file with a different extension does not become a compatible model by renaming it. Collect representative traffic, train with the runtime's supported workflow, and verify model loading before enabling anomaly inference. Logs can contain request data; configure retention and redaction for your application. 4. Choose your next task Integrate the wider Flask middleware set . Follow policy, deterministic checks, observations, and training through the architecture . Configure defaults, exemptions, and a shared backend . Operate Python training and state . Upgrade an existing installation . Checkpoint You can locate request observations, distinguish them from counters/models, and identify what must be verified before a production rollout. Previous: Add a route policy Next: Understand the architecture

title: Add a route policy
text: First protected app / Step 5 of 6 Add a route policy A route policy lets you change one check on one route. Here you will add a preview endpoint that bypasses rate limiting while the existing message endpoint retains its limit. 1. Import the selective exemption helper Change the AIWAF import at the top of app.py: from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF, aiwaf_exempt, aiwaf_exempt_from 2. Add the preview route Insert this handler before the final AIWAF(app, ...) registration: @app.get("/api/preview") @aiwaf_exempt_from("rate_limit") def preview(): return {"message": "Preview has no rate limit"} Also add this explicit preview budget before the final AIWAF registration. It keeps the baseline at three requests even after manifest inference, so five successful requests demonstrate the decorator exemption: # Pin the preview budget too; its decorator selectively bypasses that check. app.config["AIWAF_PATH_RULES"].append( {"PREFIX": "/api/preview", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}} ) The Flask route decorator is outside the AIWAF decorator. aiwaf_exempt_from disables the named check on this handler, while aiwaf_exempt on health marks a full exemption. The example selects rate limiting and logging; adding other checks later requires reviewing the preview route's intended policy. 3. Regenerate and restart aiwaf init --framework flask --app app:app python -m flask --app app:app run --port 5000 Stop the earlier server before starting another one. Run the four-request message test again: its fourth request should still be 429. Then request preview five times: python -c "from urllib.request import urlopen; print([urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/preview').status for _ in range(5)])" [200, 200, 200, 200, 200] Using a different path gives a different default rate bucket; five successes exceed the three-request threshold and demonstrate the selective exemption. Complete app after this change Show the final app.py app.py """Local learning app. Its small limits are for the tutorial, not production.""" from flask import Flask from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF, aiwaf_exempt, aiwaf_exempt_from app = Flask(__name__) app.config.update( AIWAF_USE_CSV=True, AIWAF_DATA_DIR="aiwaf_data", AIWAF_RATE_WINDOW=60, AIWAF_RATE_MAX=3, AIWAF_RATE_FLOOD=100, AIWAF_PATH_RULES=[ {"PREFIX": "/api/message", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}}, ], AIWAF_LOG_DIR="aiwaf_logs", AIWAF_LOG_FORMAT="json", ) @app.get("/api/message") def message(): return {"message": "Hello from a protected route"} @app.get("/health") @aiwaf_exempt def health(): return {"ok": True} # Added in the tutorial's route-policy chapter. @app.get("/api/preview") @aiwaf_exempt_from("rate_limit") def preview(): return {"message": "Preview has no rate limit"} # Pin the preview budget too; its decorator selectively bypasses that check. app.config["AIWAF_PATH_RULES"].append( {"PREFIX": "/api/preview", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}} ) AIWAF(app, middlewares=["rate_limit", "logging"]) Checkpoint Message remains limited, preview skips rate limiting, and health keeps its deliberate full exemption. Previous: Verify a rate limit Next: Read logs and plan training

title: Discover your routes
text: First protected app / Step 3 of 6 Discover your routes Route discovery records the routes your application actually registers. It does not create handlers or launch a permanent server. AIWAF can use the generated manifest when building route policy. 1. Import the live application Open a second terminal in aiwaf-demo , activate the same environment, and run: aiwaf init --framework flask --app app:app app:app means “import the module app.py, then read its app object.” A file path such as --app app.py is invalid. If your application uses a factory, use its import target, such as app:create_app . 2. Inspect the manifest python -m json.tool .aiwaf/paths.json You should see a JSON document with schema metadata and a routes collection containing /api/message and /health . Flask's static route may also appear. Counts and context hashes depend on the registered application; they are not fixed tutorial constants. Discovery can change effective policy The manifest includes inferred protections, not just path names. An API route may receive a suggested rate budget such as 120 requests per minute. The explicit /api/message rule in app.py takes precedence for that same prefix, keeping the tutorial limit at three. Review inferred settings before using a generated manifest in an existing app. 3. Check the imported route table If your routes are missing, inspect the module the command is loading: python -c "import app; print(app.__file__); print(*sorted(r.rule for r in app.app.url_map.iter_rules()), sep='\n')" The file should be the app.py you just created, and the route list should include both handlers. An unregistered blueprint or a different module named app cannot contribute the intended routes. 4. Know when to regenerate Regenerate after adding, removing, or changing routes. Restart the development server after generation so later requests use the updated manifest. CLI discovery imports your app and requires its dependencies and configuration to be available. Checkpoint .aiwaf/paths.json contains your live routes, and you know how to verify the import target. Previous: Create your first protected app Next: Verify a rate limit

title: Verify a rate limit
text: First protected app / Step 4 of 6 Verify a rate limit A successful response tells you the handler ran. To verify enforcement, also cross the configured boundary and inspect the response AIWAF returns before the handler. 1. Start with a fresh counter Stop the server with Ctrl+C and start it again: python -m flask --app app:app run --port 5000 The tutorial uses a process-local rate cache, so restarting clears its counters. Keep one development server running and send requests from one client. A production shared cache has a different lifetime. 2. Send four requests Create a file named verify.py beside app.py with the code below. It uses Python's standard library, so it works without curl and does not need browser headers for the tutorial's selected checks. verify.py """Run against a fresh tutorial server on port 5000.""" from urllib.error import HTTPError from urllib.request import urlopen for number in range(1, 5): try: with urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/message") as response: print(number, response.status, response.read().decode().strip()) except HTTPError as response: print(number, response.code, response.read().decode().strip()) with urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:5000/health") as response: print("health", response.status, response.read().decode().strip()) python verify.py For a fresh counter, the statuses should be: 1 200 {"message":"Hello from a protected route"} 2 200 {"message":"Hello from a protected route"} 3 200 {"message":"Hello from a protected route"} 4 429 {"error":"too_many_requests"} Whitespace in JSON may differ. The fourth request is throttled; it does not execute the message handler. This is a rate-limit response, not an anomaly-model prediction or a permanent blocklist entry. 3. Check the exempt route python -c "from urllib.request import urlopen; r=urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health'); print(r.status, r.read().decode())" 200 {"ok":true} The health handler remains reachable even while the message route is throttled. Wait for the 60-second window to expire, or restart this local teaching app, before repeating the message test. If your result differs First request is already 429: earlier requests used the same bucket; wait for the window or restart the local app. Every request returns 200: verify middleware selection, the loaded app file, the path, explicit route overrides, manifest-inferred budgets, and exemptions. Another running server may be answering on port 5000. You see 403: this tutorial does not select header/keyword checks. Check for different configuration, persisted blocks, or an upstream WAF. Connection refused: check that the first terminal is still running and the port matches. Checkpoint You have observed both a permitted handler response and an enforced rate boundary. Previous: Discover your routes Next: Add a route policy
